text: Found it: the timezone plugin's `dayjs.tz(input, tz)` treats every input as a wall-clock local time, so a Date/timestamp/Day.js input (an absolute instant) gets shifted by the target offset. Fixing it so non-string inputs are converted as instants (matching `moment.tz`). Verifying now.

Confirmed: in the timezone plugin's `tz()` the offset difference is computed from a sub-second timestamp and never rounded, so a fractional-second input yields offsets like `-420.0069` minutes, which `Z` formats as `+08:59`. Adding rounding. ETA ~5 min.

Looking at the `nl` locale's ordinal handling (the `Do` format token uses the locale's `ordinal` function); I'll make it pick the correct Dutch suffix per number. Will confirm with the existing locale tests.

Fixed in src/plugin/timezone/index.js: `dayjs.tz(input, tz)` now detects non-string input (Date, timestamp, Day.js object) and converts it as an absolute instant via `dayjs(input).tz(tz)`, instead of treating it as wall-clock time. Verified: `dayjs.tz(new Date('2020-08-07T12:00-07:00'), 'America/Vancouver').format()` → '2020-08-07T12:00:00-07:00', same for timestamp and Day.js inputs; string parsing unchanged. Full suite (524 tests) green.

Fixed in src/plugin/timezone/index.js: the offset difference is now `Math.round(...)`ed and the input's milliseconds are carried over (`$set('millisecond', this.$ms)`), so no fractional-minute offsets. Verified: `dayjs('2020-08-06T03:48:10.258Z').tz('Asia/Tokyo').format('Z')` → '+09:00', format → '2020-08-06T12:48:10+09:00', millisecond() → 258 (matches moment-timezone across many zones/values). Full suite green.
